title: Outreach & appointment setting
brief_markdown:
Modules 2 to 4 built tooling: a narrative, materials, a list. This module is the work the tooling exists for: LinkedIn notes, emails, calls and voicemails, repeated per name until a 20-minute conversation sits on a calendar. Nobody gets good at this by reading; you get good by doing a hundred reps and watching what comes back. Polishing the deck cannot be rejected, which is why founders keep doing it. Stop. For the next two weeks the only number that matters is meetings booked.

### You are selling a meeting, not Myda
Every touch has one goal: 20 minutes with the person who owns creator-video quality at a TikTok Shop agency or brand. Not a beta sign-up, not a price, not a yes. A first date earns a second date; proposing on the first one ends it. Your edge over any hired rep: you are the people building the thing, and "I'm one of the founders, I'm trying to understand how agencies handle creator feedback" lowers the guard. Keep it commercial, though. Dana must know this is about a pain she has and a product she could pay for, not a university survey.

### Start from the maths
Work backwards from meetings. Say the two of you want four first meetings a week. If roughly one in ten names that gets a full sequence agrees to a call, forty new names enter a sequence each week, twenty per founder. Each name gets six or seven touches over two weeks, so on a normal day each of you sends or dials thirty-odd touches. That is the real volume, and it is why the twenty LinkedIn requests a day you already send become step one of a sequence rather than the whole effort. The ratios are guesses you replace after week one; writing the targets down is not optional, because the Friday review only works against a number.

### Sequence, not single email
One message almost never books a meeting. Decision-makers read snippets, not essays, so the four-step drip from the materials pack is the backbone: step one short with the biggest number, steps two and three one value bucket each, step four the beta-tester story or the goodbye. Reply in the same thread every time, so a Head of E-commerce who opens step three scrolls up and reads step one, the only one you personalised by hand. Reply rates on cold sequences typically peak on the second touch and hold for several more before fading, and an explicit "last one from me" makes the people who meant to reply actually reply. When the sequence ends, the name goes into a 90-day re-queue, not the bin.

Timing beats wording. Nobody reads you in Monday-morning triage. Tuesday to Thursday around 10:00 local, early morning on the phone, or after 19:00 is when a short email reads as interesting rather than as another task. Call agency founders like Dana at the start or end of the day; midday is client calls. For US brands, follow 10:00 across the time zones.

### Personalise the first touch, automate the rest
A first message with visible evidence that a human looked at this account roughly doubles reply rates against a merge-field blast, and across a sequence the gap widens. Two minutes a name: open their TikTok Shop, watch two of their creators' videos, write one line about the hook they reuse or the brief that was clearly missed. Merge fields carry the rest (brand, category, rough creator count). Add social context when it is free: a shared 2nd-degree connection, a post they wrote last week. The trap is spending five minutes on steps two to four. The leverage is in the first touch only.

### Instrument everything
Open and click tracking on before the first send. The click target in every template, the two-minute video, exists so you see interest before a reply. Opens from two cities means it was forwarded. A re-open two days later means they are still thinking about it: call now. The morning call list is yesterday's openers and clickers first.

### Calling
Most dials do not connect, so a call is usually a voicemail, and a voicemail is an audio email: 20 seconds, with the real email landing in the same hour so they can just hit reply. Brands may have a gatekeeper; small agencies do not. Be pleasant, ask by first name, ask for the direct line.

When someone picks up, you have about 30 seconds and the phone script's bullets. Three outcomes:

- **Yes.** Get the calendar out while she is on the phone: "Are you in front of your calendar? Thursday or Friday morning?" Two to three days out; beyond a week attendance decays. Confirm her email, ask for her mobile, ask who else should be on it (her head of content). Never "I'll email you some times"; that is how booked meetings die. "I have time now" gets a demo-lite: discovery and a preview, then book the proper one.
- **Hard no.** Hear it as not now. Restate the goal once in her words, give her the out, and if she takes it retreat on your terms: you will be in touch when the timing is better. Rejected-call email within the hour. Never argue.
- **Objections, which is most calls.** "Call me next quarter": trade 30 seconds now for never bothering her again if it is irrelevant. "No budget": the call is about how her team handles feedback today, not buying. "Send me something": happy to, but a personalised pack takes 30 minutes, so 30 seconds first to check it is worth her reading; if she is clearly qualified, sell the call as the faster way to get what she asked for. "We use ChatGPT" or "we have an agency": she has just admitted the pain and the spend; grant the strength, name the gap in one sentence, ask for the 20 minutes. Feature questions are interest: close on a slot instead of answering. "What does it cost?": depends on her creator volume, which is what the call establishes. "Not my decision": tell her who you would go to next and see whether she corrects you.

Write down every objection and the answer that worked. The FAQ in the materials pack grows from this list and nowhere else.

### Book it properly
The invite comes from you, within the hour. Title "Myda × {Agency} — 20 min on creator feedback"; meeting link in both location and description; three-line agenda; one teaser link, not enough to replace the call; every attendee she named. Block 15 minutes before and after on your own calendar. Calendar reminder at 15 minutes only; anything earlier reads as "this is now". The real reminder is a short email the morning of the call repeating what she said she wanted to see. No-show: call at five past, email at fifteen with two new slots; a second no-show goes back into the sequence as not now.

### Cadence is what makes you do it
Alternate channels across two weeks, for example: day 1 LinkedIn request plus email one; day 2 call and voicemail; day 4 email two; day 7 call; day 9 email three; day 12 call and voicemail; day 14 goodbye. Break the cadence whenever a signal arrives and call that person first. The pattern matters less than having it written down and working through it; the system does the remembering so you do the dialling.

### Warm intros and inbound
Connect with your engineering co-founder, your mentors and your beta testers on LinkedIn, and every target's profile shows who you both know. Send the introducer the forwardable email from the materials pack, all asks for one introducer in one note. If they CC you, move them to BCC and propose times within the hour; if the target goes quiet, one more message in the same thread, then move on. Intros are a boost, not the engine. Your outbound will also create inbound: make sure the site's "request the beta" button lands somewhere you both check. Module 6 takes it from there.

### This week
Each of you takes twenty names from the Module 4 list, runs the full sequence with a hand-written first touch, logs every action, and on Friday you compare touches, replies and meetings per channel side by side. Two founders running the same sequence on the same segment is the fastest A/B test you will ever get.

**What you build in this module:** the outreach playbook — weekly activity targets with the maths behind them, the multi-touch sequence built from the materials templates, two-minute personalisation hooks per segment, a response-handling table with the exact next action for every reply type, the appointment-setting mechanics from proposing times to the no-show rule, what gets logged after every touch, and the Friday review with the first numbers to beat.

**Drill:** cold call to Dana, who has never heard of Myda and is between two client calls; two minutes to earn a 20-minute meeting with her and her head of content, and she will reach for "send me something".

build.spec_markdown:
Produce {{company}}'s outreach playbook, section by section, in this order. Work one question at a time; record each section with update_artifact as soon as it is good enough, then move on. This playbook consumes two earlier artifacts and must not rewrite them: the segments, qualification signals, CRM stages and 20-name list come from the icp artifact (Module 4); every message, call script and voicemail comes from the materials artifact (Module 3). If a section needs a template that does not exist in materials, note `TODO: add to materials` rather than writing it here.

1. **Targets and the maths.** Start from the end: how many first meetings per week do the two founders need, derived from the beta goal in the company artifact (how many beta customers by when, and what share of first meetings become beta starts). Then walk back with stated assumptions: sequence-to-meeting rate (start at one in ten for 2nd-degree LinkedIn names, one in twenty for cold email, mark both `assumption`), touches per name, working days. Output a table per founder per week: new names entering a sequence, connection requests, emails, calls, voicemails, meetings booked, plus the hours per day this costs. Push back if the hours do not fit beside product work; cut names, not touches per name.
2. **The sequence.** A day-by-day table over two weeks: day, channel, which materials template (3a, 3b, 3c, 3e step n, phone script, voicemail), the one value bucket that step leads with, and the send window (local time, weekday). Alternate channels; the last touch is the explicit goodbye. State the stop rule (sequence complete, hard no, or wrong person), the re-queue rule (90 days after the goodbye), and the break-cadence rule: which signals (accepted request, open, click, re-open) pull a name out of the schedule and into today's call list. Add the warm variant: when a shared connection exists, which step is replaced by the forwardable email (3d) and how long to wait before falling back to cold.
3. **Personalisation hooks.** For each ICP segment (at minimum agency and brand), two or three hooks that take under two minutes a name using only public sources: their TikTok Shop creator videos, the client roster on their site, a recent LinkedIn post, a job ad for a content role, a shared connection. For each hook: where to look, what to note, and the one fill-in sentence that goes into step one. Test: would Dana or Marcus be able to tell it was written for them? Reject hooks that need a login, a tool, or more than two minutes.
4. **Response handling.** A table with one row per reply type: interested; "send me something"; "not now / next quarter"; "no budget"; "we use ChatGPT / an agency"; "what does it cost?" and "is it free?"; "not my decision / wrong person"; feature questions; silence with signals (opened, clicked); silence without signals; hard no; bounce or left the company. Columns: what it usually means, the exact next action, within how long, which template or phone-script branch, and the CRM stage it moves to. Every row ends in a concrete ask for the 20-minute call or an explicit exit. Push back on any row whose next action is "follow up" without a date and a channel.
5. **Appointment setting.** The rules once someone says yes: propose two slots within five working days while still on the phone or in the same reply, never "I'll send times"; the invite goes out within the hour from the founder's own calendar with the title format, link in location and description, three-line agenda, one teaser link, every named attendee; 15 minutes blocked before and after; calendar reminder at 15 minutes only; the morning-of confirmation email in three sentences repeating what the prospect said they wanted; the no-show rule (call at +5, email at +15 with two new slots, second no-show returns to the sequence as not now); and the demo-lite rule for "I have time now". Write the invite body and the confirmation email as fill-in text.
6. **CRM logging.** What is written after every touch, in the CRM stages the icp artifact defined: contact, segment, hook used, touch number, channel, date, signal seen, reply type, next touch date, owner. Then the stage transitions this playbook triggers (name added, in sequence, replied, meeting booked, meeting held, not now, hard no, wrong person) so the pipeline count in Module 8 is honest. The rule from the book stands: if it is not logged, it did not happen.
7. **Weekly review.** The Friday table per founder: names added, touches by channel, connection-accept rate, email open, click and reply rates, call connects, meetings booked, meetings held, no-shows, objections heard (tallied by type). The first targets to beat are the numbers from section 1; after week one the actuals replace them. Name the three decisions the review makes: fix the list (low open or accept rate), fix the message (opens but no replies), or fix the volume (everything converts but there is not enough of it). Owner and time of the review.

Standards to enforce on every section: every number is either measured, derived from a stated assumption, or marked `assumption`; every next action has a channel, a template and a deadline; nothing here pitches the product, everything sells the call; no template text is rewritten here. Both founders run the same sequence on the same segment in week one so their numbers compare. Mark the artifact done only when all seven sections exist, the targets table has hours per day in it, and both founders would start the sequence on Monday.

drill.scenario: Cold call, day 2 of the sequence: your LinkedIn request went out yesterday and Dana has not looked at it. She picks up her mobile between two client calls, has never heard of {{company}} and did not expect the call. You have the phone script's bullets, one researched fact about her agency or its creators, and about two minutes. Your only goal is a 20-minute call within the next five working days with her and her head of content, booked while she is on the phone, not 'I'll email you some times'. She will reach for 'send me something' and 'we're pretty happy with our process', and she may ask 'is it free?'. She is warm and conflict-avoidant, so a vague 'let's definitely chat' is not a booked meeting.
drill.buyer_opening: Hello, Dana speaking? Sorry, who's this? I've got a client call in a few minutes.

rows.criterion: Opened with name, founder, and why Dana specifically (one researched fact about her agency or its creators) in under 15 seconds
Acknowledged the unexpected call and asked for two minutes, without apologising for calling
Stated the problem in agency-owner terms, specific to TikTok Shop creator videos (feedback rounds, missed briefs, client complaints), not 'content is hard'

Handled 'send me something' or 'we're happy' the chapter's way: traded 30 seconds now for not chasing her later, or sold the call as the faster way to get what she asked for; neither folded nor argued
Asked one qualifying question (creator volume, who gives feedback today) and let Dana answer it
Proposed a specific slot within five working days, 20 minutes, with her head of content, while she was on the phone, never 'I'll email you times'
Confirmed the next step out loud before hanging up: invite today, who is on it, her email confirmed, asked for her mobile
Sold the meeting, not the product: no feature tour, no price discussion, no single seller turn longer than about 20 seconds

rubric.below_threshold_note: Below 10: repeat the drill with the same persona when you can; the next module is open either way. Carry forward the weakest row as the standing fix, and add every objection Dana used that was not handled to the response-handling table in the outreach playbook and to the FAQ list in the materials artifact.
